This is NBC News. Goodbye, Louis, King of Jazz. This is Wilson Hall. Louis Sachmo Armstrong, jazz trumpeter, was buried today near the Queens, New York home, where he had lived for 30 years. The funeral service was held in a small, simple, red-brick congregational church in Armstrong's neighborhood. Only 500 could get into the church. 2,000 mourners stood outside in the summer's sweltering heat. Al Hibbler, an old friend and musician, recalled the old New Orleans days of Armstrong by singing, When the Saints Go Marching In. Father McManus of the New York Catholic Diocese gave an invocation. The pastor of the Corona Congregational Church, the Reverend Robert E. Sherrard. As ministers of this church, we welcome you to share in this tribute to the memory of the life of Louis Armstrong. It is difficult for us in this community and in this church to fashion words that would speak to you our innermost and our deepest feelings. And perhaps this would be needless in a way because anything that we would say today would be unmatched by the life and the gift that we have known and shared in the voice and the horn of Louis Armstrong. However, very briefly, I would just like to say, especially to those of you who are young and whose life is yet before you, that we have a legacy that is left to us by Mr. Armstrong. And very briefly, I would say perhaps the uppermost thing that you would want to say to the young today, to not neglect that gift that is in you. Lee Armstrong had a gift and he was born at a time when it was not very easy to live. We know of hardships and disappointments in our day and time at this moment in history, but it was even more so difficult for a man to stir up that gift that is within him and to keep his eyes on goals that would lift him above his immediate situation. So his legacy would be, I would say, I would say, Mr. God, you have a gift and man don't neglect it. Secondly, I would think that he would, would it be said, that to use that gift to bring joy and happiness. We would not make light of death at any moment. It is a mystery for the most part to most of us, but I would hate very much to see this tribute turn into one that is grounded in sorrow. Louis Armstrong used his gift to bring joy and happiness to countless millions around the world. I remember some time ago he said that when he was traveling in the Congo, when he arrived there, those cats were out there in the field shooting at each other. When they heard old pops, those cats dug it, they dropped their guns and came up to the car shouting, Moe, Satchimo, moe, Satchimo. So this is the kind of thing I think that we want to remember out of the life of Louis. And to his wife, as word of comfort, as a minister of his congregation, I would say to you, though, he may be absent in the flesh. You know more than any of us those things that kept your hands to the plow, that brought you the kind of life that you can enjoy now, that enabled you to overcome the disappointments and the sorrow and the burdensome travels of your early experiences together. Hold on to faith and to hope and to love, because when all else is done, they will remain. And finally, we all should remember these words that he uttered, I think, at his last public appearance. I want to thank the Lord, said Mr. Armstrong. I want to thank all of you, for you all have been good to old Satchimo. Louis Armstrong had requested two musical numbers for his funeral service, when the saints go marching in, and his favorite, the Lord's Prayer. Peggy Lee sang it.

Fred Robbins, a jazz critic, was the last person outside the family who saw the King of Jazz last Sunday on his 71st birthday. Robbins talked about the man and his music. Alas, poor world. What treasure thou hast lost. Whom the gods love die young, no matter how long they live. One of the world's greatest men is gone. One of the last of the true giants. Who is an artist of such extraordinary ability that he is above all possible praise. And he is a great honor for me to pay him homage to these few words. He didn't learn to sing in Milan. He got his voice training with a New Orleans newsboy quartet. He used to chirp on the curb stone for pennies. He didn't learn to play the trumpet in a conservatory. He practiced on a battered old bugle in the New Orleans waves home for boys. His professors were the sons of old man river. The musicians who worked on the Mississippi river boats. He was born back in the slums with every possible obstacle before him. And yet his genius took him across the world to triumphs in concert halls, command performances before kings and presidents, audiences with popes, and millions of words of critical acclaim by music journals of every country. His great records have spread the gospel of jazz to every nook and corner of our planet. His influence on music, on singers, on musicians, has been tremendous. There's a little bit of pops in every one of our best popular artists. And wherever jazz is played, it's Louie's music they're playing. He was the source. Jazz is a term that is much abused. But if it has any meaning at all, it means exactly what happens whenever he lifted that horn, whenever he threw his head back and curled his voice around the song. Jazz is our great cultural contribution to the creative art of the world. He was its symbol and its greatest contributor. He made it part of a global culture. And he was nothing less than a true legend in his own lifetime. He was our most gifted and infinite creative musician. A genuine American folk hero. The true folk hero, Louie Armstrong, who came up, a little boy with a beat-up cornet, out of New Orleans, to be the acknowledged jazz king of the world. He won the world with his big trumpet, his big heart, and his gravelly voice. Louie Satchmo Armstrong, born New Orleans, July 4, 1900. Died, New York, July 6, 1971.

Louis Armstrong, I think, has influenced every musician and singer. In the past 40 years, I think that they all have, Somewhere along the way, have been influenced by Louis Armstrong. It's the end of an era of this great man. Because I'm sure in 50 years from now, or 20 years from now, Or 100 years from now, he'll be in every history book. And every child will have read about Louis Armstrong in any school, In any part of the world. He was just the greatest. He was just the greatest.

I see trees of green, red and blue and stew. I see them bloom, from me and you. And I think to myself, what a wonderful world. What a wonderful world. I see skies of blue and clouds of white. The bright, blessed day. The bright, blessed day. The dark, sacred night. And I think to myself, what a wonderful world. What a wonderful world. The colors of the rainbow. So pretty in the sky. Are also on the faces of people going by. I see friends shaking in. Saying, how do you do? They're really saying, I love you. I hear pages cry. I watch them grow. They're not much more. And I'll never know. I see friends shaking in. Saying, how do you do? They're really saying, I love you. I hear pages cry. I watch them grow. They're not much more. Then I'll never know. And I think to myself.

Now, Louis Armstrong's wonderful world is just a little of Louis' Fred Robbins. I'm so glad I went to see Louis Armstrong on Sunday, his birthday, 71st, at his home in Corona. I never would have forgiven myself if I hadn't. I was on the way back from the beach and we called, of course, in advance to find out if he was okay. And his wonderful wife, Lucille, said, sure, drop in. I'd been at his home several times before on his birthday. But this was the most important. He looked fine. His face was fuller. He was having his chicken dinner, watching television. We spent about an hour with him. And he was in wonderful spirits. He talked about going back to work in the fall in Las Vegas. And that he'd been warming up on his horn every day. He felt better. His appetite was fine. And then he went through quite a siege in the hospital. Didn't really know how sick he was. Had all the nurses in stitches, telling him stories as he always did. Later, of course, they told him how seriously ill he was. He said, I guess it just wasn't my time, Pops. And then the next day it was his time. He was such a remarkable man. Really a big kid. And a very simple man. And a man that just exuded love for everybody, all kinds of people. And people loved him in return. If you mentioned Louie's name anywhere, it would provoke a smile. That was the image. Fun and jollity and goodness. I guess he was probably the greatest goodwill ambassador our country has ever had. There's no question of that. He did more for the good name and the good feeling toward America than anybody. And in every corner of the world. And if you stop and think, he is or was the most famous American in the world. Better known than anybody. Any scientist, any sports figure, any motion picture star. The best known American any place in the world. Everyone knew Louie Armstrong. The amazing thing about Pops is that with all that success and fame and adulation and adoration and the fact that he played for kings and had audiences with popes and had been everywhere, he was really a simple, unpretentious man. He had a modest home in Corona, Queens where he's lived for 30 years. A marvelous wife, Lucille, whom he met at the Cotton Club. Gave him 30 years of great, great happiness. And I guess it was just innate in his character to have this wonderful humility about him, despite his greatness. The stories, the mother wit that he had, the earthy humor, was also very much a part of Pops. He was one of the greatest storytellers ever. You could mention any subject. Anybody's name, he'd have a story about it. And he'd have you rolling on the floor. And what jokes, you know. Really a happy man all through his life. But in a world that has so much turmoil, the most important thing to Louis was love. He knew that that was what the world needs then and now. Love. And he spread a lot of joy to the world through his great artistry, his playing, his singing, his incomparable performances everywhere. He spread a lot of sunshine around. He made the world a better place for having been in it. He was loved. And, of course, he'll be missed terribly. Because everything came from him. He was the source. The best popular artists today is a little bit of Louis in all of them. Anybody who plays jazz anywhere, I mean, Pops laid it down.

segments.title: Singers as stylists: Cab Calloway, Fats Waller and Armstrong's trumpet power
segments.summary: Barker and the host discuss singers as individual stylists, Cab Calloway's Jewish-flavored material, and why Armstrong moved from cornet to trumpet, with his barrel chest and power.

segments.title: Broadcast music and Armstrong walking the streets of Harlem and Chicago
segments.summary: Song clips of New Orleans material and station jingles frame the interview; Barker starts describing Armstrong being mobbed on the streets in the 30s and 40s.

segments.title: Armstrong's warmth with people, Europe, New Orleans pride and James Brown
segments.summary: Barker recalls Armstrong greeting everyone, his dressing room, red beans and rice, his rolling with the punches, his acclaim in Europe like Bechet, Barker's return to New Orleans, the coming funeral at the armory, and the comparison with James Brown.

segments.title: Danny Barker on his guitar playing and wish to be a writer
segments.summary: The host asks Barker about himself; he talks about playing rhythm guitar in New York bands and being a frustrated writer.

segments.title: Armstrong cannot be figured out; his temper and the dozens
segments.summary: Barker says there is only one Armstrong, ranks him above Caruso, Edison and Ford, recalls his temper and mastery of the dozens, and the interview closes.

segments.title: NBC News report on Armstrong's funeral in Queens
segments.summary: Wilson Hall reports the funeral service, the minister's eulogy, hymns by Al Hibbler, Peggy Lee and Hugh Porter, and Fred Robbins's tribute to Armstrong's life and influence.

segments.title: Fred Robbins's eulogy for Armstrong
segments.summary: Fred Robbins pays tribute to Armstrong's New Orleans roots, genius and global influence on jazz.

segments.title: Blueberry Hill and Armstrong on Heebie Jeebies scat origin
segments.summary: After Blueberry Hill, archival clips of Armstrong explain how dropping the lyric sheet in the studio led to wordless scat singing.

segments.title: Monitor tribute: Satchmo nickname, Doc Severinsen and Lucille
segments.summary: Murray the K introduces clips including Armstrong explaining the origin of Satchmo, his generosity on stage, and a message to Lucille.

segments.title: Armstrong as New Orleans king and Oscar Cohen's tribute as road manager
segments.summary: A New Orleans speaker tells of Armstrong's Rex toast to the King of England, followed by Oscar Cohen recalling being his road manager and his influence.

segments.title: Fred Robbins recalls his last visit with Armstrong
segments.summary: After What a Wonderful World, Fred Robbins describes visiting Armstrong at home on his 71st birthday and his humility, humor and love.
